15310:
To strut means to walk in a proud, confident, and deliberately showy way. It is not ordinary walking — it is performing while walking. When someone struts, their chest is pushed out, their chin is up, their shoulders are pulled back, and their steps are bold and deliberate. Every single movement sends a message to the world: "Look at me."

A peacock spreading its feathers and parading around is the perfect visual image of strutting. In fact, that image is so connected to this word that you will often hear people say someone "strutted like a peacock."

Strut is not just a physical action — it is powered by an emotion. The person strutting feels proud, superior, or extremely pleased with themselves. They want to be seen, noticed, and admired. The walk is an outward expression of an inner feeling of importance or triumph.

People strut when they feel on top of the world — after a victory, when they look great, or when they feel superior to others around them. For example:

  • A footballer who scores a crucial goal might strut across the pitch toward his teammates.
  • A model does not simply walk the runway — she struts down it.
  • Someone who just got a big promotion might strut into the office the next morning.
  • A musician stepping onto a huge stage in front of thousands might strut out from the wings.
Is It a Compliment or a Criticism?

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word: strut sits in the middle ground between confidence and arrogance, and the context of the sentence decides which side it leans toward.

When it is positive: It suggests healthy self-confidence, self-celebration, and power. The person is owning the moment and commanding attention in an admirable way.

"She strutted onto the stage, completely in her element."
Here, you feel admiration for her.

When it is negative: It suggests showing off, arrogance, or an inflated sense of self-importance — the kind that irritates people around you.

"He strutted around the office like he owned the place."
Here, you feel slightly annoyed by him.

The word itself does not change — only the surrounding context and the speaker's tone tell you whether the strutting is cool or obnoxious.

• After winning the award, he strutted up to the podium with a huge grin on his face.
  • She put on her new outfit and strutted around the room, admiring herself.
  • The rooster strutted through the yard, chest puffed out, ignoring everyone.
  • Don't strut around just because you got lucky once.
  • The athletes strutted out during the opening ceremony, beaming with national pride.
The Very Common Phrase: "Strut Your Stuff"

You will encounter this phrase constantly, so it is essential to know it. "Strut your stuff" means to confidently show off your skills, talents, looks, or abilities — to put yourself on display and own it without apology.

"This is your moment. Go out there and strut your stuff!"

It is almost always used in a positive, encouraging way — like a coach pushing a performer to go give it their all with full confidence.
How Strut Differs from Similar Words

Since English has many words for "walk," knowing how strut is different from its neighbours is crucial.

Walk is completely neutral. It carries zero emotion or attitude — you are simply moving from one place to another.

March is purposeful and disciplined, like a soldier. It is about forward momentum and duty, not pride or self-display.

Saunter is slow, relaxed, and carefree — the walk of someone who has nowhere urgent to be and is perfectly at ease. There is no showing off involved.

Swagger is the closest relative to strut, and the two are often confused. Swagger also implies an attitude-filled, confident walk, but it carries a stronger sense of arrogance and defiance — often with a side-to-side rocking motion of the body. Swagger feels more street-wise and rebellious, while strut feels more theatrical and proud.

Strut is the one that most clearly screams self-importance, pride, and a desire to put on a show.

If you need to compress everything above into a single sentence: to strut is to walk in a deliberately proud and showy way, driven by a feeling of superiority or triumph, with the clear intention of being seen and admired.
15311:
A stub is something that is cut short, broken off, or left over — a small piece that remains after most of something is gone. Think of it as the leftover, the remnant, or the short blunt end of something that was once fuller or longer.

This core idea branches out into several related meanings, all of which share that same feeling of "a small, shortened piece."
1. A Physical Remnant (the most direct meaning)

When you use something up until very little of it is left, that tiny remaining piece is a stub.

  • After writing with a pencil for weeks, you're left with a pencil stub — a short, blunt piece barely worth holding.
  • After a candle has burned almost completely down, the small waxy remains at the bottom is a candle stub.
  • After smoking a cigarette, the short leftover piece that you extinguish is a cigarette stub (sometimes called a "butt").

The common thread: something that used to be whole and full has been used up, cut down, or broken, and what's left behind — that short, blunt, sometimes awkward leftover — is a stub.

The word also applies to things that were always short by nature, not just worn down. A tree branch that was cut close to the trunk and left as a short protruding bump is a stub. A short, broken tooth (or a baby tooth that's partially worn) is called a stub. A short, thick nail that's been hammered down almost flush — same idea.
2. A Stub as a Record or Counterfoil (the "kept piece" meaning)

Here, a stub is the small detachable portion of a larger document that you keep as proof or a record after the main part has been torn away or used.

Imagine a paper ticket for a concert. It has two parts connected along a perforated line: the main ticket (which gets taken at the door) and a smaller piece on one end. After an attendant rips off the main portion, you're left holding that smaller piece. That's your ticket stub. It's proof you attended. People often keep them as souvenirs.

The same logic applies to:

  • Check stub (or check counterfoil): In a checkbook, when you write a check and tear it out, the thin strip that stays behind in the book is the stub. You write on it what the check was for and the amount — it's your personal record.
  • Pay stub: The slip of paper (or digital document) you receive alongside your salary payment, showing the breakdown — your gross pay, taxes deducted, deductions, and net pay. Even if the payment itself goes directly into your bank account, the pay stub is your record of how that amount was calculated. This is one of the most common uses of the word in everyday life.
  • Receipt stub, lottery stub, etc. — same idea in different contexts.

The defining feature here: the stub is always the smaller, retained portion — it's what's left after the main piece is gone, and it functions as a record or reference.
3. A Stub in Computing and Software Development (the placeholder meaning)

In the world of programming and software, a stub takes on a slightly different but related meaning: it's a minimal, incomplete piece of code that stands in for something that hasn't been built yet — or that deliberately does nothing (or does the simplest possible thing).

Imagine a team of developers is building a large application. Developer A is writing one piece of the program, and that piece needs to call a function that Developer B is supposed to write. But Developer B hasn't written it yet. So Developer A creates a stub — a placeholder function with the right name and structure, but with an empty body or a simple fake response (like always returning zero, or always returning "success"). This lets Developer A keep working without being blocked.

In the same way, when you're testing software, you sometimes don't want to call the real version of a function (maybe it costs money, connects to a live database, or is slow). So instead, you use a stub — a simplified fake version that behaves in a controlled, predictable way just for the purposes of the test.

The connection to the other meanings is clear: just like a pencil stub is an incomplete, reduced version of a full pencil, or a ticket stub is the small remaining portion of a full ticket — a code stub is an incomplete, bare-minimum version of a full piece of code.
4. A Stub in Networking and APIs (a close cousin to the programming meaning)

In distributed computing and networking, a stub is a small piece of code on one side of a connection that acts as a representative or stand-in for a service located elsewhere (often on another machine or server).

For example: when your app makes a request to a remote server, your app itself doesn't know all the low-level details of how to communicate across the network. A stub handles that — it sits on your side, looks like a normal function you can call, but behind the scenes it packages your request and sends it over the network. The stub is your local representative for something that lives far away.

This is a narrower, more technical meaning, but the core idea holds: a stub is a small, reduced stand-in for something larger or more complex.

Every meaning of "stub" (as a noun) circles back to the same intuition:

Something that is short, reduced, or incomplete — either the remnant of something larger, a small piece kept after the whole is gone, or a simplified placeholder standing in for something more complete.

SituationWhat the stub is

Whether you're looking at the nub of a worn pencil, the slip in your wallet from last year's concert, the salary breakdown from your employer, or a placeholder function in a codebase — in every case, a stub is small, partial, and either what remains or what stands in.
A Quick Feel for the Word in Sentences

• "I found an old concert ticket stub at the bottom of my bag."
  • "The pay stub showed that a lot was deducted for taxes this month."
  • "The developer wrote a stub for the payment function until the real implementation was ready."
  • "All that was left of the candle was a small wax stub."
  • "He stubbed his toe on the door — wait, that's the verb. As a noun: the broken, blunt stub of the old fence post jutted out from the ground."

The word carries a slight connotation of incompleteness or inadequacy. A stub is never the full thing — it's always the lesser, shorter, reduced version. This is why in software, a stub is considered temporary: it's a stand-in until the real thing is built. And in everyday life, a pencil stub is what you use when you can't find a proper pencil. There's a mild sense of "this is not ideal, but it'll do."

That feeling — the small, blunt, leftover piece that makes do — is the soul of the word.
15312: Stubble refers to short, stiff, rough bristles or stalks that are left behind after something has been cut down or shaved off. The word captures a very specific texture and appearance — something that is not smooth, not long, but short, sharp, and a bit prickly.

Stubble is used in two main real-world contexts, and once you understand both, the word becomes very clear.

1. Stubble on a farm (crop stubble)

When a farmer grows wheat, barley, rice, or any other grain crop, the plant grows tall. When harvest time comes, the farmer cuts down the crop to collect the grain. But the farmer doesn't cut all the way to the ground — a few centimetres of the lower stalk are left behind, sticking up from the soil.

Those short, dry, sharp leftover stalks that remain in the field after harvesting are called stubble.

If you've ever walked through a harvested wheat field, you know what this feels like. The ground is covered with hundreds of these short, stiff, yellowish stalks poking upward. They are rough and can even scratch your legs if you walk through them. The field looks patchy and rough — not smooth like a lawn, not tall like a crop. This in-between, rough, leftover state is exactly what stubble is.

"After the harvest, the fields were full of stubble, dry and golden under the autumn sun."

2. Stubble on a face (facial stubble)

This is the more commonly used meaning in everyday conversation today.

When a man shaves his face, the skin becomes completely smooth. But hair grows back. After about one to three days without shaving, the hair hasn't grown long enough to be called a beard — it's still very short. These short, rough, slightly prickly hairs covering the jaw, chin, cheeks, and upper lip are called stubble.

Facial stubble has a very recognisable texture. If you touch it, it feels rough and scratchy, almost like sandpaper or the surface of a hairbrush. It's not soft like a full beard, and it's not smooth like clean-shaven skin. It's that in-between, bristly stage.

"He hadn't shaved in two days, and there was dark stubble across his chin and cheeks."

"She noticed the stubble on his jaw when he leaned in to talk."

Stubble on a face is often associated with a certain rugged or casual look. Some people deliberately maintain this short-hair look rather than shaving clean or growing a full beard — this is sometimes called designer stubble or simply keeping a stubble beard.

Both uses of stubble share the same core idea:

  • Something was once longer or fuller.
  • It was cut down or removed.
  • What remains is short, rough, stiff, and bristly.

Whether it's the leftover stalks in a harvested field or the regrown hairs on an unshaved face, the word captures that specific texture and appearance perfectly. Think of stubble as nature's sandpaper — rough, short, and left behind.

To truly own this word, hold this image in your mind:

  • Visually: Not smooth, not long. Patchy, rough, uneven.
  • To the touch: Prickly, scratchy, bristly — like tiny stiff needles.
  • In mood: Slightly unkempt, rugged, raw, natural.

Here are some natural, real-world examples:

  • "The stubble on the harvested field made it hard to walk barefoot."
  • "He rubbed the stubble on his chin thoughtfully."
  • "Her cheek felt scratched after he kissed her because of his stubble."
  • "The fields were reduced to stubble after the combine harvester moved through."
  • "He had three days' worth of stubble — not quite a beard yet."

From stubble, we get the adjective stubbly, which simply means covered in stubble or having the quality of stubble.

  • "His stubbly face scratched my hand."
  • "The stubbly field looked bare after the harvest."

A stubble field refers specifically to a farm field after the crops have been harvested and only the short stalks remain. This phrase is common in literature and descriptions of the countryside, especially in autumn.

Stubble is the word for the short, rough, prickly bristles or stalks that remain after something — a crop or facial hair — has been cut, giving a scratchy, uneven texture to whatever surface they cover.
15313:
Imagine you are trying to convince a friend to change their mind about something. You give them good reasons. Other people agree with you. The facts are clearly on your side. But your friend simply will not budge. They keep saying "No, I'm right, and I'm not changing my mind." That person is being stubborn.

Stubborn means refusing to change your mind, your opinion, or your behavior, even when there is a good reason to do so. The key word here is "even." A stubborn person is not just firm — they resist changing especially when they are being pressured, corrected, or shown that they might be wrong.

"Stubborn" is not a neutral word. It carries a negative tone most of the time. When you call someone stubborn, you are usually criticizing them — suggesting that their refusal is unreasonable, illogical, or frustrating. It implies that they are holding on to their position not because they have thought it through carefully, but simply because they do not want to change.

This is what separates stubbornness from words like "determined" or "persistent," which are generally positive. A determined person works hard to reach a goal. A persistent person keeps trying despite difficulty. But a stubborn person resists change or persuasion — and that resistance often has no good reason behind it.

This is the most common use. A stubborn person:

Refuses to admit they are wrong, even when the evidence is clear. Sticks to a decision no matter what others say. Will not compromise or meet someone halfway. Keeps doing things their own way even when a better way is shown to them.

For example: "My grandfather is so stubborn that he refused to see a doctor even when he was clearly sick." Here, the stubbornness is dangerous and unreasonable — he is hurting himself by refusing to budge.

Or: "She stubbornly insisted on walking home alone even though it was raining heavily." Again — a refusal to change course despite good reasons.

Here is something interesting: "stubborn" is also used for non-human things — problems, stains, illnesses, objects. In this case, it means something that resists being removed, solved, or changed — just like a stubborn person resists being persuaded.

For example:

"That is a stubborn stain — it won't come out no matter how much I scrub."
"He has had a stubborn cough for three weeks."
"The stubborn lock finally gave way after several hard tries."

In each case, the idea is the same: something that refuses to go away or change, even when you are trying hard to make it do so.

Rarely, and only in specific situations. Sometimes, a person's stubbornness is admired — especially when they are refusing to give up on something worthwhile, like a cause, a dream, or their values, despite great opposition.

For example: "She stubbornly refused to abandon her community, even when everyone else had left."

Here, the stubbornness sounds almost heroic. But notice — even in these cases, the writer is borrowing the word's edge of "refusing to change" and applying it to something we happen to respect. The word itself still carries a slight sense of hardheadedness. It does not fully shed its critical tone. Words like "resolute" or "unwavering" would be cleaner compliments — "stubborn" used positively always has a small ironic twist to it.
How Stubborn Compares to Similar Words

Obstinate means almost exactly the same thing as stubborn, but is even stronger and more formal. It suggests an especially unreasonable, deeply fixed resistance. If stubborn is a 7 out of 10 on the scale of refusal, obstinate is a 9.

Pig-headed is very informal and quite rude. It means someone is stubborn in a dumb, mindless way — like an animal that won't move. You would use this among friends, not in formal writing.

Headstrong means a person who is determined to do what they want and does not like being told what to do. It is very close to stubborn, but leans slightly more toward impulsiveness — acting on your own strong will — rather than simply refusing to change.

Determined and persistent are the positive cousins. They share the idea of not giving up, but they describe admirable qualities — working hard, not quitting. Stubborn, by contrast, describes unreasonable resistance.

The opposite of stubborn is someone who is flexible, open-minded, or accommodating — a person who listens to others, considers new information, and is willing to change their position when it makes sense to do so.

"Stubborn as a mule" — a very common expression meaning extremely stubborn. Mules are famously difficult animals to move or direct, which is why they are used as the comparison.

"Stubborn refusal" — a very common pairing. A stubborn refusal is a firm, unmoving "no."

"Remain stubborn" / "stay stubborn" — used to describe someone who keeps their position over time.

"A stubborn problem" — a problem that is very hard to solve and keeps persisting.

Stubborn means refusing to change your mind or behavior, even when there is a good reason to — and it is usually a criticism, suggesting the refusal is unreasonable or frustrating, whether describing a person, an illness, a stain, or anything else that simply will not yield.
15314:
Something is stubby when it is short and thick at the same time — shorter than you'd normally expect, and wider or chunkier than its own length would suggest.

The two qualities go together. Something short is not automatically stubby. Something thick is not automatically stubby. But when something is both short and thick, especially when it looks like a compressed, squished-down version of what it's supposed to be, that's when the word "stubby" fits perfectly.

Imagine a brand-new, full-length candle. Now imagine that same candle after it has burned down almost completely — now it's just a short, squat, wide little thing sitting in its holder. That is stubby.

Or think of a pencil. A fresh pencil is long and thin. After months of sharpening and using, what's left is a tiny, thick, hard-to-hold piece. That leftover piece is stubby.

The shape of "stubby" is essentially: wider than it is long, or thicker than its short length would call for. Things that are stubby often look like they didn't quite finish growing, or were worn or cut down from something longer.
What Can Be Described as Stubby?

Body parts are probably the most common use:

  • Fingers and toes — If someone has short, thick fingers — not long and slender, but compact and wide — those are stubby fingers. They look like little sausages rather than long, tapered fingers.
  • Legs — The Corgi dog is famous for having stubby legs. The legs work perfectly well, but they are noticeably short and thick relative to the dog's body.
  • A tail — A dog with a naturally short or docked tail has a stubby tail — just a small, dense little nub.
  • Teeth — Teeth that have been worn down over time, or are just naturally short and blunt, can be called stubby.
  • Arms — A person or animal with short, thick arms relative to their body has stubby arms.

Objects can also be stubby:

  • A crayon that has been used down to a tiny piece is stubby.
  • A bottle that is shorter and wider than the standard shape can be called stubby. (In Australian English, "stubby" is actually also used as a noun for a short, fat beer bottle — but as an adjective, it just means looking like that shape.)
  • A screwdriver with a very short handle is a stubby screwdriver (this is even a real product name in tools).
  • A candle, pencil, or stick that has been worn or burnt down to a small, thick piece is stubby.

Animals are frequently described this way:

  • Short-legged dog breeds like Corgis, Dachshunds, and Basset Hounds are known for their stubby legs.
  • A caterpillar's short, stumpy prolegs (the small leg-like structures on its belly) could be called stubby.
  • A bird with proportionally short, wide wings has stubby wings.

Plants too:

  • A plant with short, thick little branches rather than long, reaching ones has stubby branches.
  • A tree cut down to just a short, thick base has a stubby trunk.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Stubby is mostly a neutral, descriptive word. It is fairly casual and conversational — you'd use it in everyday speech or informal writing rather than in formal or academic writing. It paints a clear physical picture without being dramatic.

When used about objects or animals, it usually sounds neutral or even a little endearing. A puppy with stubby legs is often considered cute. A stubby little bottle of hot sauce might look charming.

When used about a person's body parts, it can sound slightly unflattering, because it implies that those parts didn't reach the typical length. Calling someone's fingers "stubby" is not the kindest thing. It's not a harsh insult, but it's blunt enough to be noticeable. So in conversation, the word is worth using carefully when referring to people directly.
How It's Different From Similar Words

Understanding what makes "stubby" unique becomes clearest when you compare it to words that look similar:

Stubby vs. Short
"Short" only tells you about length — nothing else. "Stubby" tells you about both length and thickness. Stubby fingers are short and thick. Short fingers might just be small but still slender.

Stubby vs. Thick
"Thick" only tells you about width. Thick fingers are wide, but they might still be long. "Stubby" adds the information that they are also short.

Stubby vs. Stumpy
This is the closest comparison. Both words mean short and thick. The difference is in tone and context. Stumpy tends to feel slightly stronger, slightly more negative or comic, and is often used for whole limbs (a stumpy leg, a stumpy arm). Stubby is a little gentler and is used for a wider range of things, including small objects like pencils and bottles.

Stubby vs. Squat
"Squat" describes the overall shape of something that is wide and low — like a squat building or a squat little jar. It tends to refer to the shape as a whole. "Stubby" is more often used for individual parts or elongated things (fingers, legs, tails, bottles, pencils) that are compressed or shorter than expected.

Stubby vs. Chunky
"Chunky" focuses on bulk and heaviness. It doesn't necessarily say anything about length. A chunky dog is big and heavy-set, but could have long or short legs. A stubby dog has legs that are specifically short and thick.

Stubby vs. Blunt
"Blunt" describes an end that is dull or flat — not sharp or pointed. Stubby things often have blunt ends (like a worn-down pencil), but "blunt" alone says nothing about length or thickness. The two words are related in feel but describe different qualities.

You can adjust the degree of stubbiness:

  • Stubbier — more stubby than something else. "The Dachshund has stubbier legs than the Labrador."
  • Stubbiest — the most stubby in a group. "Of all her colored pencils, the red one was the stubbiest after weeks of drawing hearts."

Here are some natural sentences to see the word working in context:

  • "He struggled to type quickly because of his stubby fingers."
  • "The puppy wagged its stubby little tail furiously when it saw her."
  • "She rummaged through her bag and found only a stubby piece of eyeliner pencil."
  • "The hedgehog trotted forward on its stubby legs, completely unbothered."
  • "They handed me a stubby bottle of artisanal sauce — short and fat, with a wide label."
  • "The old tree had been cut down, leaving just a stubby stump in the ground."
  • "The mechanic used a stubby screwdriver to reach the bolt in the tight corner."

Stubby = short + thick, where the shortness is noticeable and the thickness is proportionally high relative to that short length. The word paints a picture of something compact, dense, and squatter than the standard or ideal form. It's a neutral-to-casual word, used freely about objects and animals, and with a little care when talking about people's bodies.
15315: The word stud has several distinct meanings. Each one is used in a completely different situation, so the key is to learn them one by one. Once you can picture each context, the word will click naturally.
1. A Small Decorative Metal Knob

This is probably the most visually straightforward meaning. A stud here is a small, rounded piece of metal that is attached to or pressed into a surface — usually leather or fabric — to decorate it. Think of those shiny silver dots you see on biker jackets, belts, or boots. Those dots are studs.

They stick out slightly from the surface, like tiny bumps. Their purpose is mostly decorative, though they can also reinforce material.

"She wore a black leather jacket covered in silver studs."
2. A Type of Earring

A stud earring (most people just call it a "stud") is a small earring that sits flat and snug against the earlobe. It doesn't hang down like a drop earring, and it doesn't circle the ear like a hoop. It simply rests close to the skin, held in place by a tiny backing that clips on from behind the ear.

Stud earrings are extremely common and come in many materials — gold, silver, diamond, plastic, and so on.

"She wore small pearl studs to the interview."
"My ears were newly pierced, so I stuck with simple studs."
3. A Structural Beam Inside a Wall (Construction)

In building and construction, a stud is one of the vertical wooden (or metal) beams that form the hidden skeleton — the internal frame — of a wall. Imagine a wall as being like a human body: the drywall or plaster you see is like the skin, but underneath there are "bones" holding everything up. Those bones are the studs.

They run vertically from floor to ceiling inside the wall, spaced evenly apart (commonly 16 inches in American construction). Once the wall is finished, you cannot see them at all — they're buried inside.

This matters a great deal in everyday life: if you want to hang something heavy on a wall (a television, a shelf, a large mirror), you must screw the mounting hardware into a stud. Drywall alone is too fragile to support serious weight. Because studs are invisible, people use a handheld tool called a stud finder to locate them behind the wall.

"Don't just drill into the drywall — make sure you hit a stud."
"The carpenter marked where each stud was before hanging the shelves."
4. A Male Breeding Animal (Especially a Horse)

A stud is a male animal — most commonly a horse (a stallion) — that is kept and used specifically for breeding. The idea is that this animal has exceptional qualities: speed, strength, a valuable bloodline, impressive physical traits. Owners pay to have this animal mate with females so its qualities are passed on to the offspring.

A stud farm is a property where such animals are bred and raised.

A common phrase is "put out to stud" — this means a male animal (usually a racehorse after its racing career ends) is retired from competition and kept solely for breeding purposes.

"The champion racehorse was retired and put out to stud."
"He runs a stud farm in Kentucky."

The word can technically apply to other male animals too (bulls, dogs), but horses are the most common association.
5. An Attractive, Confident, Virile Man (Informal/Slang)

In casual everyday English, calling a man a stud is a compliment. It means he is considered physically attractive, sexually confident, and impressive — someone who commands attention and admiration. The connection to the breeding-animal sense above is not subtle; the implication is similar.

This usage is very common in informal speech, pop culture, sports commentary, and casual conversation.

"All his teammates looked up to him — he was the stud of the team."
"Back in college, he was considered a real stud."

It is worth knowing that this word, in this sense, only applies to men (not women), and it carries a very masculine, almost boastful energy. It is not offensive — it is a compliment — but it is informal. You would not use it in a formal or professional setting.
6. A Metal Fastener Threaded on Both Ends (Engineering)

In mechanics and engineering, a stud (sometimes called a stud bolt) is a metal rod that has screw threads on both ends but has no head (unlike a regular bolt, which has a flat or hexagonal top you can grip with a wrench). One threaded end is screwed firmly into a surface or block, and the other end sticks out so that a nut can be tightened onto it, clamping two parts together.

You find these inside car engines, industrial machines, pipes, and anywhere two heavy components need to be firmly and precisely joined.

"The cylinder head is fastened to the engine block using head studs."
"One of the wheel studs snapped, so the tire couldn't be mounted properly."
7. Metal Pins Embedded in Winter Tires

In countries and regions with heavy ice and snow, some winter tires have small metal spikes — called studs — embedded directly into the rubber tread. These tiny hardened metal pins pierce the ice as the tire rolls, giving the vehicle far better grip on icy roads.

Tires equipped with these pins are called studded tires. They are controversial in some places because they damage road surfaces, and many regions have laws about when and where they can be used.

"He switched to studded tires before the first snowfall."
"Studded tires are banned on dry roads in some countries."
8. A Type of Poker Game

Stud (or stud poker) is a family of card games. In stud poker, each player is dealt a mix of face-down cards (private — only that player sees them) and face-up cards (public — everyone can see them). This is different from Texas Hold'em, where community cards are shared in the middle of the table.

The two most popular variants are Five-Card Stud and Seven-Card Stud.

"They sat down for a few hands of seven-card stud."
9. A Collar Stud (Historical, Now Rare)

A collar stud is a small, button-like metal fastener that was once used to attach a detachable collar to the body of a dress shirt. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, men's shirts often had separate, removable collars (they could be laundered independently), and collar studs were the hardware that held them in place.

This is an almost entirely historical meaning. You are unlikely to encounter it in modern life unless you are reading older literature or watching period dramas. If a character in a Victorian novel fumbles with his collar stud, now you know what he is doing.

"He hurried to fasten his collar stud before the guests arrived."
Quick Mental Map

Since the word looks the same regardless of which sense is meant, context is everything. Here is an easy way to remember which meaning applies:

  • Leather jacket / belt / boots → decorative metal knob
  • Ears / jewellery → earring
  • Wall / drilling / construction → hidden wooden beam
  • Horse / breeding → male animal for reproduction
  • Man / admiration / slang → attractive, virile guy

15316:
When "studied" is used as an adjective, it means deliberately done, carefully thought out, and intentional — the opposite of natural, spontaneous, or accidental.

If something is studied, it means a person has consciously decided to do it or project it. There is effort behind it. It didn't just happen on its own.

Here is what makes "studied" special and different from simply saying "deliberate" or "intentional":

When you call something studied, you are suggesting that the person worked at it — they crafted it, rehearsed it, or maintained it with conscious effort — often to create a specific impression on others. The result may look effortless or natural on the surface, but underneath, there is careful construction.

Think of it like an actor who has practiced a facial expression until it looks real. The expression is studied — it is not genuinely spontaneous, it is performed with intention.

"a studied indifference"
This is the most classic use. It means the person is deliberately acting as if they don't care. They are not genuinely indifferent — they are performing indifference, with effort. Perhaps they don't want others to see that something bothers them, so they carefully project a cool, unbothered attitude.

She greeted her ex-boyfriend with studied indifference, pretending she had long moved on.

"a studied calm"
The person is not naturally calm in this moment. They are working to appear calm — holding themselves together with intention.

Despite the chaos around him, the general spoke with studied calm, refusing to show panic.

"a studied insult"
This is not an accidental or careless remark. The insult was crafted — chosen carefully, delivered precisely to sting.

His "compliment" was actually a studied insult, designed to humiliate her in front of everyone.

"a studied response"
The answer was not off the cuff. It was prepared, rehearsed, and controlled.

The politician gave a studied response that revealed nothing about his actual views.

"a studied neglect"
The person is deliberately ignoring something — it is not forgetfulness, it is a conscious strategy.

Her studied neglect of his messages was her way of sending a message without saying a word.

"Studied" often carries a slightly cool or even faintly negative connotation. When you describe something as studied, you are quietly hinting that it is not fully authentic — that there is a gap between what is being shown and what is truly felt or meant.

It signals: this did not come naturally; this was constructed.

For example:

  • A "genuine smile" is warm and real.
  • A "studied smile" is a smile that has been put on with intention — perhaps to seem friendly, but it is not arising from true warmth.

This is why "studied" is often used to describe behaviors that are strategic, diplomatic, or even manipulative — behaviors where someone has decided how they want to come across and then worked to project exactly that.
Who or What Gets Described as "Studied"?

Typically, "studied" describes:

  • Expressions and attitudes — studied nonchalance, studied calm, studied indifference, studied cheerfulness
  • Language and responses — a studied answer, studied politeness, a studied remark
  • Actions and behavior — studied neglect, studied avoidance
  • Style and appearance — a studied casualness (someone dressed to look effortlessly stylish, when in fact they spent an hour on it)

You will almost never use "studied" to describe a physical object. It describes human behavior, manner, or expression — things that can be performed or controlled.
How It Differs from Similar Words

WordWhat it emphasizes

"Deliberate" simply means done on purpose. It has no judgment attached. "He made a deliberate choice."

"Calculated" suggests cold logic and self-interest. "Her kindness was calculated."

"Affected" means unnatural and pretentious — usually with a negative judgment. "His accent sounded affected."

"Studied" sits in between — it means consciously constructed and intentional, with a quiet suggestion that the naturalness is performed. It is more elegant and neutral than "affected," but it still hints that something has been crafted rather than felt.
A Simple Way to Remember It

If someone's behavior is studied, they are like a student who memorized their lines perfectly — they deliver the performance with control, not because it flows naturally from them, but because they worked at it.

The word quietly asks: Is this real, or is this crafted? And it leans gently toward: crafted.

"Studied" (adjective) = done with deliberate effort and intention, often to create a specific impression, and usually implying that what is shown on the outside has been carefully controlled rather than arising naturally from within. It describes behavior, manner, or expression that is performed with thought, not spontaneous.
15317:
When you call someone studious, you mean they spend a lot of time studying, reading, and learning — and they do it with genuine focus, care, and dedication. A studious person doesn't just open a book reluctantly; they actively engage with learning. They pay close attention, they go deep into what they're learning, and they take it seriously.

Think of it this way: if "lazy" and "distracted" sit on one end of a scale, "studious" sits firmly on the other end.

"Studious" actually carries two related but slightly different meanings depending on how it's used. Both come from the same spirit — careful, deliberate, focused effort.

1. Describing a Person Who Loves Learning

This is the most common use. A studious person is someone who:

  • Genuinely dedicates themselves to study and learning
  • Reads and works diligently, not because they're forced to, but because they value knowledge
  • Is focused and serious when it comes to academic or intellectual work

"She was a studious young woman who always had a book in her hand."

"The library was full of studious students preparing for their exams."

The word carries a quietly positive, respectful tone. Calling someone studious is a compliment — it suggests discipline, seriousness, and a love of knowledge.

2. Describing a Careful, Deliberate Action or Effort

This is a slightly more formal use of the word. Here, "studious" means done with very careful, conscious attention — almost like someone is making a point of doing something deliberately.

"He made a studious effort to remain calm during the argument."

(= He very carefully and deliberately worked to stay calm.)

"She gave the documents a studious reading before signing."

(= She read the documents with thorough, focused attention.)

In this sense, the word describes the quality of attention or effort — not a person's general character, but a specific careful action.
What "Studious" Implies — The Feeling Behind the Word

When you call a person studious, you're saying more than just "they study." You're suggesting:

  • They have a habit of studying — it's a consistent part of who they are, not a one-time thing
  • They approach learning with seriousness and care, not casually
  • There's a certain quietness and focus to them — studious people are not usually the loudest in the room

A studious person is the one in the library while others are out. They take notes carefully. They revisit what they've learned. They ask questions and seek understanding.

It's worth clearing up a few things so you use this word accurately:

  • Studious does not mean "intelligent." A person can be very smart but not studious (they might be gifted but lazy). Equally, someone can be studious without being exceptionally gifted — they simply work hard and study diligently. The word is about effort and habit, not natural ability.
  • Studious does not mean "bookish" in a negative way. While it can suggest someone who prefers studying over socializing, the word itself is not negative or critical. It is neutral-to-positive in tone.
  • Studious does not mean "obsessed." It means dedicated and diligent, not unhealthily fixated.

You can also use "studious" in degrees to shade your meaning:

  • "He is quite studious" — fairly dedicated to study
  • "She is remarkably studious" — unusually dedicated, in an impressive way
  • "He is not particularly studious" — he doesn't study much or with much seriousness

Knowing these will sharpen your understanding of studious by showing you its "neighborhood" of meaning:

  • Diligent — hardworking and careful (broader; applies to any kind of work, not just study)
  • Scholarly — focused on academic knowledge; often implies deep expertise
  • Earnest — sincere and serious in effort
  • Conscientious — taking care to do things correctly and thoroughly
  • Academic — related to learning and study (more about the subject area than the person's behavior)

Of these, diligent is the closest in feel, but studious specifically centers on learning and study, while diligent can apply to any kind of hard work.

• Idle / Lazy — not putting in effort
  • Inattentive — not paying careful attention
  • Careless — doing things without proper focus or care
  • Unmotivated — lacking the drive to learn or work

If you want to say...Use "studious" when...
A person who works hard at studying"She is a studious learner."
An action done with careful attention"He gave it a studious look."

Studious is a word of quiet discipline. It describes someone — or an effort — marked by focused, dedicated, and careful attention to learning and knowledge. It's a respectful word, a compliment, and a precise one.
15318: "Stuffy" has three main meanings. What's beautiful about this word is that a single idea quietly connects all three: the feeling of something being closed off, blocked, or airless.
Meaning 1: A Room or Place with Bad Air

This is the most common meaning. A stuffy room is one where the air feels warm, heavy, and stale — almost like the air hasn't moved in a long time. You might feel uncomfortable, slightly breathless, or even a headache coming on. It's the opposite of a fresh, well-ventilated space.

This happens when:

  • Windows and doors have been shut for a long time
  • Too many people are packed into a small space
  • There is no fan, air conditioning, or airflow

Examples:

  • "It's so stuffy in here. Can we open a window?"
  • "The old library was stuffy and smelled like dust."
  • "After hours on the plane, the cabin felt unbearably stuffy."

Synonyms for this meaning: airless, close, stifling, muggy, unventilated.

When you have a cold, flu, or allergies, your nose gets congested — filled with mucus — and you can't breathe through it easily. In this state, your nose is described as stuffy.

This is one of the most common expressions in everyday English, especially in informal speech. You'll almost always hear this as "a stuffy nose".

Examples:

  • "I woke up with a stuffy nose and a sore throat."
  • "She couldn't smell anything because of her stuffy nose."
  • "This cold medicine relieves a stuffy nose within minutes."

Synonyms for this meaning: blocked, congested, bunged up (informal British English).
Meaning 3: A Person Who Is Too Formal, Rigid, or Old-Fashioned

This is perhaps the most interesting meaning. When used to describe a person, organization, attitude, or environment, "stuffy" means overly serious, stiff, conventional, and resistant to anything casual, fun, or new.

A stuffy person:

  • Follows rules and traditions very strictly
  • Disapproves of behavior they find too casual, modern, or relaxed
  • Is easily offended by jokes, informality, or anything unconventional
  • Tends to be boring or self-important
  • Often makes others feel uncomfortable or judged

This word carries a mildly critical or mocking tone. When you call someone stuffy, you're gently (or not so gently) criticizing them for being uptight and old-fashioned.

Examples:

  • "My uncle is so stuffy — he insists on wearing a tie even at family barbecues."
  • "The board of directors is too stuffy to consider any new ideas."
  • "She left the stuffy law firm to join a creative startup."
  • "I found the dinner party a bit stuffy — nobody laughed or relaxed."

Synonyms for this meaning: prim, pompous, stiff, strait-laced, conservative, uptight, conventional.

Notice how all three meanings share a core idea — something is closed, blocked, or unable to breathe freely:

  • A stuffy room is sealed off from fresh air.
  • A stuffy nose is physically blocked.
  • A stuffy person is mentally closed — blocked from new ideas, humor, and ease.

This connection is what makes "stuffy" such an expressive and memorable word.

"Stuffy" is moderately negative in all its meanings, but it's never harsh or rude. It's more of a gentle complaint or mild criticism. You'd use it comfortably in everyday conversation, whether talking about the weather, your health, or someone's personality.

15319:
To stultify something or someone means to drain them of vitality, intelligence, or effectiveness — to smother, dull, or make them look foolish and incapable.

This word carries a few closely related meanings that all orbit the same dark center: something active, capable, or meaningful is being crushed into something dull, absurd, or powerless.
Meaning 1: To make something dull, deadening, and ineffective

This is the most common modern use. When something stultifies a person, it slowly kills their sharpness, creativity, or motivation — not violently, but through grinding monotony, rigid restriction, or pointless routine.

Think of a brilliant scientist forced to spend every day filing paperwork instead of doing research. That bureaucratic tedium stultifies them — it doesn't destroy them outright, but it suffocates their potential until they can no longer function at their best. The key feeling here is of something vital being quietly smothered.

Examples:

  • "Years of repetitive, unchallenging work stultified her once-sharp mind."
  • "The rigid rules of the school stultified the students' natural curiosity."
  • "A culture of fear stultifies innovation — no one dares to try anything new."

Notice the pattern: something that should be alive and productive (a mind, curiosity, innovation) is being made inert and useless by an external force.
Meaning 2: To make something appear foolish, absurd, or self-contradictory

Here, to stultify means to cause something — often an argument, a claim, or a person — to look ridiculous, inconsistent, or intellectually bankrupt. This use is more formal and appears frequently in legal, academic, and philosophical writing.

When someone stultifies their own argument, they have said or done something that makes their own position look foolish or contradictory — they have undermined themselves.

Examples:

  • "By making that wild claim with no evidence, he completely stultified his earlier, well-reasoned position."
  • "Her decision to accept the bribe stultified everything she had said about honesty."
  • "The new findings stultified the professor's entire theory."

The sense here is of something collapsing into absurdity — losing all credibility or logical coherence.
Meaning 3: To render something futile or worthless (often used in formal/legal contexts)

Closely related to the above, stultify can mean to negate or invalidate something — to make it utterly pointless and without effect.

Examples:

  • "The endless procedural delays stultified any hope of a fair trial."
  • "New legislation stultified all their previous efforts."
The unifying thread across all meanings

Whether stultify is being used to describe a deadening of the mind, a collapse into absurdity, or the nullifying of effort, the word always carries the sense of something worthwhile being made worthless — something capable being made incapable, something that should work being made not to work.

It is a word with weight. It implies a kind of waste — potential that has been extinguished, arguments that have caved in on themselves, people who could have thrived but were instead ground down.
Who or what can be stultified?

• A person's mind, creativity, or spirit — through boredom, oppressive systems, or lack of challenge
  • An argument or theory — when contradictions or new evidence expose it as absurd
  • A process, effort, or movement — when something prevents it from having any real effect
  • A person's reputation or credibility — when their actions make them look foolish
The tone and register of the word

Stultify is not a casual, everyday word. You will encounter it most often in formal writing — essays, criticism, legal texts, journalism, and literature. When a writer chooses stultify over simpler alternatives like "dull," "undermine," or "negate," they are being deliberate: the word carries a richness that implies not just failure, but a kind of indignity — something active and promising being reduced to something passive and pointless.

Stultify vs. dull — "Dull" simply means to make less sharp or interesting. Stultify implies something more severe: a systematic crushing of capacity or credibility, often with a sense of waste or absurdity.

Stultify vs. undermine — "Undermine" means to weaken something gradually. Stultify is more total — it suggests rendering something completely ineffective or making it look foolish, not just weakening it.

Stultify vs. stifle — "Stifle" means to suppress or restrain. Stultify goes further: it doesn't just suppress something, it drains it of all meaning and effectiveness, or exposes it as absurd.
One sentence to remember it by

If you ever need a mental anchor for this word, think of it this way:

To stultify is to turn something capable into something useless — either by smothering it slowly from the outside, or by making it collapse into absurdity from within.

Master that, and you'll recognize and use this word correctly every time you encounter it.
